How to Spot Fake Dispensary Listings and Online Weed Scams

Fake listings, copycat websites and pay-first requests are the most common cannabis scams. Here is how to spot them, check a Michigan license and report fraud.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20265 min read

05min readNews & Culture
In this article
  1. How dispensary scams work: fake listings and copycat sites
  2. Red flags: shipping offers, payment-app requests and pressure to prepay
  3. Why licensed shops don't ship cannabis
  4. How to check a Michigan retailer's state license
  5. Where to find High Society's real store pages, hours and online menu
  6. If you already paid: bank, payment app, IC3 and FTC
  7. Protecting personal data and security codes
  8. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • Licensed Michigan dispensaries don't mail cannabis; the Postal Service considers marijuana nonmailable, even between legal states.
  • A seller who wants payment by app, gift card or wire before you ever see a store is a red flag.
  • Check any Michigan retailer in the Cannabis Regulatory Agency's license search before you trust it.
  • If you paid a scammer, contact your bank or payment app right away and report it to the FBI's IC3 and the FTC.

Dispensary scams usually start with a search result that looks right and end with money sent to a stranger. Fake search listings, copycat websites and sellers who promise to ship cannabis to your door are typical versions. The fix is simple: know the red flags, check the license and buy from a store you can walk into.

How dispensary scams work: fake listings and copycat sites

Scammers borrow what makes a real store look trustworthy. They build websites that look official, or put their own phone number next to a real business's name in search results. Some promise home delivery, take payment through an app, then add fees and disappear. Any business with a public listing can be copied, so reach a store through its own website, not a link someone sends you.

Red flags: shipping offers, payment-app requests and pressure to prepay

Walk away if a seller:

  • Offers to ship or mail cannabis to your home, in any state
  • Wants payment by Cash App, Venmo, Zelle, gift card, cryptocurrency or wire before you've seen a store
  • Pushes you to pay now, or adds surprise fees for "insurance," "customs" or a "driver"
  • Won't give a street address, or gives one that doesn't match the store's own website
  • Never mentions checking your ID

The Federal Trade Commission warns that scammers like payment apps because it's hard to get your money back once you send it.

Why licensed shops don't ship cannabis

As of October 2026, adult-use marijuana is still a Schedule I controlled substance under federal law. In 2021, the U.S. Postal Service said THC products other than hemp remain generally prohibited in the mail, even when the sender and buyer live in states that allow cannabis. Moving cannabis between states breaks federal law too.

So a "dispensary" offering to mail cannabis is either breaking federal law or planning to take your money and send nothing. Legal cannabis sales in Michigan go through licensed businesses, never the mail. Our guide to cannabis delivery in Michigan explains how that differs from a mail-order scam.

How to check a Michigan retailer's state license

Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses adult-use and medical cannabis businesses. Its Verify a License tool has separate searches for adult-use establishments and medical facilities.

  1. Search the business name or city in the agency's tool.
  2. Make sure the licensed address matches the store you plan to visit.
  3. Contact the store using details from its own website, not an ad or a text.
  4. Expect an ID check at the counter. Michigan stores check ID before every sale, and legal products carry the state's required labels.

Our guide to licensed vs. black market cannabis covers the other differences.

Where to find High Society's real store pages, hours and online menu

High Society has eight Michigan stores: Big Rapids, Birch Run, Charlotte, East Lansing, Lenox, Mount Pleasant, New Buffalo and Saline. Each store page on our website lists its own address, hours and directions, so start from our store locations page rather than a search ad.

To order ahead, pick your store on our online menu, add items and choose a pickup time, in store or curbside. Bring a valid ID each time you pick up an order. Our guide to ordering cannabis online walks through each step, and our FAQ covers common questions.

If you already paid: bank, payment app, IC3 and FTC

Act fast:

  1. Call your bank or card issuer and report the charge as fraud.
  2. Report it in the payment app. The FTC notes that Cash App and Venmo take reports through in-app chat.
  3. File with IC3. The FBI runs the Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov), the central hub for reporting cyber-enabled crime.
  4. Report to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
  5. Keep records: screenshots, usernames, phone numbers, web addresses and receipts.

Protecting personal data and security codes

  • Never share a one-time security code. The FTC says anyone who asks for the code sent to your phone or email is a scammer.
  • Don't text photos of your ID to an online seller. A licensed store checks ID in person.
  • Check the web address. A copycat site may swap a letter or add a word to a real store's domain.

Adults 21 and older, and registered medical patients 18 and older, can shop legally at licensed Michigan stores. Valid ID required. Please consume responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

Can a dispensary ship weed to my house?

No. Licensed Michigan dispensaries cannot mail cannabis. The Postal Service considers marijuana nonmailable, even between states where cannabis is legal, and moving cannabis between states breaks federal law. Any seller offering to ship cannabis to your home is a red flag, so buy in person or order ahead for pickup.

Is it safe to pay for weed with Cash App or Venmo?

Not when you're paying a seller you've never met. The FTC warns that scammers push payment apps because it's hard to get your money back. Licensed stores take payment at pickup or through their own checkout. At High Society, cash works, and other payment options vary by store.

Where do I report a cannabis scam?

Start with your bank or payment app to try to stop or reverse the payment. Then file reports with the FBI through ic3.gov and with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Save screenshots, usernames, phone numbers and receipts first, since they make your report more useful.

How do I check if a Michigan dispensary is licensed?

Use the Cannabis Regulatory Agency's online license search, which has separate lookups for adult-use establishments and medical facilities. Search the business name or city and compare the licensed address with the store you plan to visit. Licensed stores also check ID before every sale and sell products with Michigan's required labels.

Sources

  1. U.S. Postal Service: Treatment of E-Cigarettes in the Mail, final rule (Federal Register, Oct. 21, 2021), on THC-containing products being nonmailable, govinfogovinfo.gov
  2. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Verify a Licensemichigan.gov
  3. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Marihuana Rules, R 420.1 to R 420.1004 (ID check before each sale; labeling)michigan.gov
  4. Federal Trade Commission: Mobile Payment Apps: How To Avoid a Scam When You Use One (May 2022)consumer.ftc.gov
  5. Federal Trade Commission: What's a verification code and why would someone ask me for it? (consumer alert, March 7, 2024)consumer.ftc.gov
  6. FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)ic3.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
